title: Suppressing microwave crosstalk in superconducting quantum processors by designing parasitic drive capacitances
authors: Anuj Aggarwal, Jorge Fernández-Pendás, Simon Pettersson Fors, Zakaria Mohamed, Halldór Jakobsson, Amr Osman, Janka Biznárová, Andreas Nylander, Anita Fadavi Roudsari, Marcus Rommel, Anton Frisk Kockum, Giovanna Tancredi
abstract: As superconducting quantum processors scale to large qubit counts, unwanted microwave drive crosstalk becomes an important source of coherent errors. Here, we investigate the role of parasitic coupling paths in the suppression of drive crosstalk in a processor with two fixed-frequency transmon qubits and a tunable coupler. To account for the many different coupling paths, we develop a detailed circuit model to capture the dependence of crosstalk on the coupler frequency. We experimentally demonstrate suppression of crosstalk, finding that the suppression does not originate solely from cancellation of the effective qubit-qubit coupling, but also is a result of interference between other coupling paths. Building on these insights, we show that drive crosstalk can be suppressed with the right choice of parasitic capacitances, which otherwise often are treated as unwanted design imperfections. Our results provide practical guidance for low-crosstalk device design of superconducting quantum processors and point toward a broader strategy in which parasitic coupling paths are engineered rather than simply minimized.
summary: This paper addresses microwave crosstalk in scalable superconducting quantum processors by developing a detailed circuit model. The authors experimentally and theoretically demonstrate that crosstalk nulls can be engineered by strategically designing the parasitic capacitances. This shifts the paradigm from merely minimizing unwanted couplings to actively engineering these paths for improved device performance.
main_problem: Unwanted microwave drive crosstalk is a major source of coherent errors that limits the scalability of superconducting quantum processors.
main_result: Crosstalk can be suppressed by engineering the parasitic capacitances, showing that these paths can be constructively utilized rather than just minimized.
method: The authors developed detailed circuit models and used high-frequency expansions to analyze the effective Hamiltonian and cross-Rabi frequencies.
model_or_system: The system is a superconducting quantum processor featuring two fixed-frequency transmon qubits coupled by a tunable coupler, modeled using a circuit Lagrangian and analyzed via an effective Hamiltonian.
key_observables: Cross-Rabi frequencies ($R_{	ext{cross}}$) and self-Rabi frequencies ($R_{	ext{self}}$) are used to quantify crosstalk, alongside the static ZZ interaction ($\zeta_{	ext{ZZ}}$).
important_parameters: Josephson energies ($E_{Jk}$), capacitances ($C_{ij}$), and the coupler frequency ($\Phi_{	ext{ext}}$) are key parameters governing the coupling and drive response.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a high-frequency expansion truncated at first order, and initial models neglected certain parasitic couplings.
figures_summary: Figures show measured self- and cross-Rabi frequencies versus coupler frequency, demonstrating dips indicating crosstalk suppression, and compare measured/simulated Rabi oscillations.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the crosstalk problem to developing a detailed Hamiltonian model, analyzing the crosstalk via dressed drive amplitudes, and finally demonstrating experimental suppression by engineering parasitic capacitances.
why_interesting: The work provides concrete, physically grounded design rules for superconducting quantum hardware, moving beyond simple coupling cancellation to utilize parasitic elements for error mitigation.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Device micrograph with false coloring. Two floating qubits (Q1 and Q2) are coupled via a tunable coupler and a direct capacitor. Each qubit has its own XY control line and readout resonator. The full list of the device parameters is given in Table II in Appendix A.

FIG. 2. Circuit schematic of two floating transmon qubits, Q1 and Q2, capacitively coupled to a grounded flux-tunable coupler through C1c and C2c, with direct qubit–qubit coupling through C12. The node fluxes ϕ1u, ϕ1d, ϕ2u, ϕ2d, and ϕc define the five circuit nodes, where ‘u’ and ‘d’ label the up and down flux nodes of each qubit. The XY1 (blue) and XY2 (green) drive lines couple capacitively to the circuit. Solid lines indicate coupling to the target qubit, dash-dotted lines coupling to the coupler, and dashed lines coupling to the victim qubit. The corresponding drive capacitances are labeled in the schematic. We neglect the small parasitic capacitive couplings between ϕ1u −ϕ2u, ϕ1d −ϕ2d,...

FIG. 3. Experimental self- and cross-Rabi frequencies as a function of coupler frequency. (a, c) Measured self-Rabi rates of Q1 driven through XY1 and Q2 driven through XY2, respectively, as a function of coupler frequency. (b, d) Corresponding cross-Rabi rates of Q2 driven through XY1 and Q1 driven through XY2. At each coupler bias, the driven qubit is excited at its resonance frequency. Markers show the experimental data, while the solid curves show the fit given by Eqs. (19) and (20). The vertical dashed line in (b, d) indicates the coupler frequency at which Jeff = 0.

FIG. 4. Measured crosstalk for the two drive lines as a func- tion of coupler frequency, expressed in dB using Eq. (21). The quantities Λ2,1 and Λ1,2 correspond to crosstalk from XY1 to Q2 and from XY2 to Q1, respectively. More negative val- ues indicate stronger isolation between the drive line and the victim qubit. The dashed blue line indicates the stronger suppression of Λ1,2 predicted by the analytical model, which is not observed experimentally. This discrepancy may arise from additional crosstalk mechanisms not accounted for in the model.

FIG. 5. Dependence of the crosstalk-null frequencies of Rcross Q2 (blue) and Rcross Q1 (green) on the parasitic drive capacitances. (a, b) Crosstalk-null frequencies for Q2 driven through XY1 and Q1 driven through XY2 as a function of the drive-to-coupler capacitance for the floating- and grounded-qubit architectures, respectively. (c, d) Corresponding crosstalk-null frequencies as a function of the drive-to-victim capacitance for the floating- and grounded-qubit architectures, respectively. The blue circles and green squares in (a, c) indicate the fitted capacitance values from Table I for XY1 and XY2, respectively. The horizontal dashed line in (d) marks the maximum coupler frequency.
